CREATION_RULE_CONTEXT.NETWORK_ENVIRONMENT_CONSTRAINTS: Deterministic offline/local benchmark runtime; no dependence on cloud credentials, privileged external infrastructure, internet services, or destructive host routing. Simulate or namespace route operations safely while preserving realistic Linux routing semantics and Ansible-managed multi-node behavior.

inputs.REQUESTED_DOMAIN: Linux route-table and policy-routing control plane in Go, Ansible-managed fleet rollout, and network operations dashboard

CANDIDATES.ENGINEERING_OBJECTIVE: Build a production-style Go route control plane that models desired route and policy state, reconciles it across a multi-node Linux fleet, detects drift, protects management reachability, records revision history, and exposes the same lifecycle through an operator dashboard and Ansible-driven installation/configuration.
REQUIREMENT_FAMILIES: policy routing rules and named tables
fleet rollout waves and failure isolation
dashboard inventory, route, drift, rollout and revision views
CANDIDATES.SCALE_FIT: VERY_HIGH: naturally supports more than 3000 substantive runtime/configuration LOC, 20-30 coupled failure manifestations, and 25-30 distinct behavioral F2P cases without padding.
PRESERVATION_OBLIGATIONS: never mutate the host runner routing table
rejected changes leave serving desired and observed state unchanged
unchanged nodes remain stable across retries
management-safety routes cannot be removed without an explicit safe replacement
revision and audit history remains monotonic
Ansible reruns do not create duplicate service/config state
CANDIDATES.DUPLICATE_RISK: LOW_MEDIUM: Linux route CRUD and Ansible deployment are established patterns, but coupling revisioned multi-node desired state, policy rules, multipath, drift/reconcile, safety invariants, rollout/rollback, service deployment and one dashboard creates a broader and more distinctive work package than a generic netlink wrapper or router UI.

CANDIDATES.ENGINEERING_OBJECTIVE: Focus the Go service on atomic route-table plus FIB-rule transactions, dependency ordering, validation, rollback and restart recovery for complex Linux policy-routing changes.
CANDIDATES.SCALE_FIT: HIGH but narrower fleet/Ansible/dashboard surface than the requested idea.
CANDIDATES.DUPLICATE_RISK: MEDIUM: transactional network configuration is a familiar systems pattern.

CANDIDATES.ENGINEERING_OBJECTIVE: Center the system on inventory, route snapshots, drift analytics, compliance policies, remediation waves and dashboard workflows across many nodes.
CANDIDATES.SCALE_FIT: HIGH, but route mutation semantics would be less central than requested.
CANDIDATES.DUPLICATE_RISK: MEDIUM: fleet drift dashboards are common unless the routing transaction semantics remain deep.

outputs.WHY_THIS_ONE: It preserves all three requested elements as first-class coupled responsibilities rather than bolting them together: the Go API owns realistic route/policy state and transaction semantics, Ansible owns repeatable multi-node installation and variable projection, and the frontend operates revisions, routes, nodes, drift and rollouts. The Linux rtnetlink model provides authentic route/rule semantics while the benchmark can remain deterministic and unprivileged by using a kernel-model adapter instead of altering the runner's network.
outputs.DUPLICATE_RISK_NOTES: Use Linux rtnetlink route/rule semantics as public calibration, not copied implementation. Avoid cloning edge-router-runtime: this task manages host route tables and policy-routing desired state, not HTTP traffic routing. Preserve a distinct state model, API, Ansible topology and dashboard workflow.
